content: Individuals diagnosed with diabetes should be provided with blood glucose monitoring (BGM) devices tailored to their specific circumstances, personal preferences, and treatment regimens. For those utilizing continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) devices, it is essential that they also have access to BGM devices at all times as a supplementary tool. Patients who are on insulin therapy and using BGM should be encouraged to monitor their blood glucose levels at appropriate times based on their insulin regimen. This includes checking glucose levels during fasting states, before meals and snacks, after meals, at bedtime, during the night, and in relation to physical activity (before, during, and after exercise). Additionally, glucose monitoring is critical when hypoglycemia is suspected, after treating low blood glucose levels until normoglycemia is achieved, when hyperglycemia is suspected, and prior to and during the performance of critical tasks such as driving. Healthcare professionals must be cognizant of the variability in accuracy among different blood glucose meters and consider this when recommending devices to patients. Although the use of BGM in individuals not on insulin therapy has not consistently demonstrated clinically significant reductions in A1C levels, it can still be a valuable tool. BGM may assist in making adjustments to meal plans, physical activity routines, and/or medications, particularly those that carry a risk of hypoglycemia, as part of a comprehensive treatment adjustment program.
